The Tana River mangabey (Cercocebus galeritus) is a medium-sized primate endemic to the fragmented gallery forests of southeastern Kenya, and its life-history traits reflect a relatively slow pace of life typical of many cercopithecids. Gestation in this species, measured through captive observations of a single well-studied female, lasts approximately 175 days [tg = approximately 175 days] when the individual is maintained at a stable core body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], a duration that is consistent with the gestational periods reported for other members of the tribe Papionini. Following parturition, the altricial neonate, weighing an estimated 425 grams [Wwb = 425 grams] based on comparative data from the closely related Lophocebus albigena, is entirely dependent on maternal milk for its initial nutritional requirements. This birth mass is modest relative to the female's ultimate adult size, reflecting a typical primate pattern of small neonatal mass invested in a single offspring per reproductive event.

A much larger proportion of somatic growth is accomplished during the pre-weaning and juvenile periods, which are characterized by intensive maternal care and progressive nutritional independence. At a normothermic body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], weaning is estimated to occur at approximately 365 days after birth [tx = approximately 365 days after birth], a figure that marks the transition to exclusive reliance on solid foods and the cessation of regular suckling. The prolonged nursing phase, which exceeds twelve months after birth [tx = exceeds twelve months after birth], is energetically demanding for the mother and is thought to be linked to the species' reliance on a high-quality but patchily distributed diet of hard fruits and seeds that young infants cannot process independently at a temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. The extended period of maternal investment is a common feature among forest-dwelling cercopithecids, where slow infant development correlates with complex social learning and the acquisition of foraging skills within a stable group context.

Sexual maturation in C. galeritus follows a protracted developmental trajectory, with puberty documented to begin at approximately 2267 days after birth [tp = approximately 2267 days after birth] under the thermal conditions of a stable core temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This represents an age of roughly 6.2 years, a value that places the species near the upper end of the maturation schedule observed among comparably sized mangabeys and mandrills. The delay in reaching reproductive maturity is likely related to the need for females to attain a sufficient body size to support gestation and lactation, as well as the competitive social environment in which young males must establish rank before gaining mating access. Captive records indicate that males continue to grow well beyond the onset of puberty, eventually reaching a substantially larger ultimate body size than females, a pattern consistent with pronounced sexual dimorphism in this genus.

Body size dimorphism is a striking feature of the Tana River mangabey, with the ultimate wet weight for adult females in captivity recorded at 6285 grams [Wwi = 6285 grams], while adult males attain a significantly greater ultimate wet weight of 10183 grams [Wwi = 10183 grams]. This nearly 1.6-fold difference in body mass between the sexes is comparable to that observed in other highly dimorphic papionins, such as the mandrill (Mandrillus sphinx), and is thought to result from intense male-male competition for access to receptive females. The substantial mass gained by males continues well into adulthood, with cranial crests and body musculature becoming increasingly prominent with age, suggesting that selection favors larger body size in males as a determinant of fighting ability and reproductive success within multimale-multifemale social groups.

Reproductive output in this species is heavily constrained by the long interbirth intervals that follow each parturition. Females typically produce a single infant per birth event [N_R_i = single infant per birth event], and the frequency of these events is low, with females giving birth approximately once every 24 months [F_R_i = birth approximately once every 24 months]. This slow reproductive schedule, combined with a maximum lifespan of 24 years [am = 24 years] recorded in captivity at a stable core body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], results in a lifetime reproductive output that is low relative to smaller, faster-lived primates, underscoring the vulnerability of this species to population declines driven by habitat fragmentation and reduced female survivorship.
